title: Adult Learning Theory: Design for the People Doing the Work

lessons.title: 1. Begin with the work, then test your assumptions
lessons.transcript:
Allow 4 minutes, including the decision and check. Fictional case: Harbor Service Desk is introducing a shared handoff form. A usable handoff contains an issue summary, the next owner, and the next action. Ten sampled handoffs contain four missing owners. The manager requests a presentation about the new process. Before building it, ask what people must do and what prevents them from doing it.

Andragogy, associated with Malcolm Knowles, offers assumptions concerning adults' need to know why, self-direction, experience, readiness, problem orientation, and motivation. These are useful questions for design, not guarantees about each adult. An experienced employee may be a novice with this tool; someone attending a mandatory session may need substantial guidance. Adult learning has multiple theoretical perspectives, and andragogy is not its single universal explanation. See the Penn State readings in Sources.

Worked example: replace “They are adults, so let them explore” with “Can they already locate the owner list and submit a practice handoff?” Observe the task, ask about obstacles, and offer a guided example when needed. In this sample, the instructional goal is a complete handoff. Fixing access to the owner list belongs in the implementation plan too.

Now it's your turn. A capable new supervisor asks for a step-by-step demonstration before practicing. What should you do? Pause the video and make your choice in the activity below.

paragraphs.title: Check readiness through a real task

lessons.title: 2. Use experience without preserving errors
lessons.transcript:
Allow 4 minutes. Prior experience is useful evidence, but familiar habits can conflict with a changed workflow. Carnegie Mellon’s learning principles describe prior knowledge as potentially helpful or obstructive. A designer needs to uncover both useful knowledge and inaccurate assumptions.

Worked example: a veteran agent says, “I put the owner’s name in the notes, as we always have.” In the fictional new process, routing reads the Owner field; notes do not trigger assignment. Start by asking the agent to show the old workflow. Identify what remains valid, such as a concise issue summary. Then contrast two handoffs with the same notes but different Owner fields. Have the learner predict which will route correctly and explain why.

Avoid framing the veteran as resistant or assuming tenure equals mastery. The old behavior may have been correct under the previous system. Feedback can acknowledge the reasoning while correcting the action: “Your summary makes the issue clear. Routing now uses the Owner field, so select the owner there before submitting.”

Pause for 30 seconds: identify one thing that should stay the same and one thing that must change in a process you know. If using Harbor, preserve the issue summary and change how the owner is assigned.

Now it's your turn. An experienced agent’s demonstration reveals an outdated shortcut. Choose the strongest response. Pause the video and make your choice in the activity below.

lessons.title: 3. Offer relevant choices and the support to succeed
lessons.transcript:
Allow 4 minutes. Relevance is more than adding a workplace photograph. In this sample, it means practicing the decision that creates a usable handoff. Motivation may include doing useful work, confidence, recognition, or simply meeting an employment requirement. Do not assume everyone arrives enthusiastic or motivated in the same way.

Worked example: replace a long department history with a short opening: “By the end, you will choose an owner and next action for a handoff so another agent can continue the case.” Let learners select a password-reset or order-status case. Both use the same required fields and performance criterion. Offer a text example, optional demonstration, and a readily available checklist. These options support access and task needs; they do not label people as fixed visual, auditory, or kinesthetic learners.

Choice has boundaries. A learner may choose a relevant practice case, but cannot skip a required safety or privacy control. An experienced user may need less explanation, while a novice may need the complete walkthrough. Check performance rather than relying only on confidence ratings.

Mini-design task: choose a workplace example for a novice and one for an experienced colleague. Keep the assessed requirement identical. Write one sentence explaining why each example is relevant.

Now it's your turn. You have novices and experienced agents in one session. Which plan best balances choice and common expectations? Pause the video and make your choice in the activity below.

Design two routes to one requirement

lessons.title: 4. Make practice resemble the decision
lessons.transcript:
Allow 4 minutes. A learner who can name the fields may still struggle to use them. Practice should expose the choice that matters, then provide feedback the learner can use in another attempt. Carnegie Mellon’s learning principles emphasize goal-directed practice and targeted feedback.

Worked example: fictional request “A customer cannot access an invoice. The billing system is available, and the account has been verified.” The practice rule says invoice-access cases go to Billing Support; the next action is to check the invoice permission. A complete handoff states the issue, names Billing Support in the Owner field, and records that next action. Show one completed example, then ask the learner to resolve a different case using a short rule card.

An early attempt can include hints. A later attempt should remove unnecessary help while keeping tools people normally use at work. Explain the consequence of a wrong selection and invite a retry; “Incorrect” alone does not show how to improve.

Decision practice here is deliberately low risk. Use fictional records, not actual customer information. The final multiple-choice assessment samples decisions; it does not verify live-system proficiency. A production rollout would also need observation of representative handoffs.

Now it's your turn. The objective is to route handoffs using a rule card. Which practice is best aligned? Pause the video and make your choice in the activity below.

paragraphs.title: Fade help without removing job tools
Use safe practice and honest claims

lessons.title: 5. Plan transfer and measure what changed
lessons.transcript:
Allow 4 minutes. Course completion is an implementation measure. It does not establish that handoffs improved, or that any improvement was caused by the course. A useful plan separates learning evidence, workplace behavior, and conditions that enable the behavior.

Worked example: before the fictional rollout, inspect a comparable sample of handoffs for all three required elements. During training, collect decision-check results. After rollout, inspect another comparable sample and record missing elements. Ask supervisors whether staff can access the owner list, have time to complete the form, and receive consistent expectations. A simultaneous form redesign could also explain changes in performance.

Give the team a one-screen handoff checklist. Ask managers to review the first few attempts, correct errors privately, and route tool-access problems to the system owner. If staff can perform correctly in practice but lack production permissions, another explanation video will not grant those permissions.

Transfer task, 60 seconds: write a plan containing one practice task, one support available at the point of work, one responsible person, and one observable behavior to review. Sample: “Agents route two practice cases; the team lead pins the rule card and reviews whether next week’s sampled handoffs name an owner.”

Now it's your turn. Agents pass practice but cannot open the owner list in production. What should the rollout lead prioritize? Pause the video and make your choice in the activity below.
